title: What Am I Doing?
theme: Naming familiar actions through pretend play
materials: A few simple objects that make an action easy to recognize, such as an empty plate and spoon, an empty cup, a book, or a toothbrush.
instructions: Choose two or three familiar actions and simple objects that help show each one. Take turns pretending to do an action. For example, pick up an empty plate and spoon and pretend to eat. Ask, "What am I doing?" and pause for a few seconds. Accept any word or approximation connected to the action, then say the action clearly yourself: "Eating!" Then switch turns. Let your child use one of the objects while you name or guess what they are doing. Continue with a few familiar actions while your child is interested.
success_criteria: The child attempts to say at least one action word during the game.
make_easier: Use very familiar actions with clear objects: a spoon and plate for eating, a cup for drinking, a book for reading, a toothbrush for brushing. Model the action word first if needed, then repeat the pretend action and give your child another opportunity.
make_harder: Remove the objects and act out a familiar action using only your body, such as pretending to eat, drink, sleep, wash, or read. Pause and let your child figure out the action from your movements. You can also let your child act out an action for you to guess.
group_play_line: Take turns being the person who acts and the person who guesses.
what_to_avoid: Do not repeat the question over and over if your child does not answer. Model the action word and keep the pretend play moving.

title: What Are You Doing?
theme: Naming the child's own action during everyday play
materials: Whatever your child is already using, such as crayons, cars, a ball, blocks, pretend food, or a snack.
instructions: Watch what your child is already doing and wait for a natural pause. Ask, "What are you doing?" Give your child a few seconds to answer. Accept any word or approximation connected to the action, then model the action clearly — "Coloring!", "Eating!", "Drinking!", "Playing cars!", or "Playing ball!" Use the question occasionally so the interaction stays conversational rather than feeling like a test.
success_criteria: The child attempts to say a word or short phrase describing what they are doing.
make_easier: Offer two clear spoken choices based on the activity, such as "Are you playing or coloring?", "Are you eating or drinking?", or "Are you playing cars or playing ball?" Pause. If the child points, looks, or chooses correctly without saying the action, acknowledge the understanding, model the action word or phrase, and give another opportunity to say it. A nonverbal choice does not count as expressive success.
make_harder: Ask the open question without giving choices: "What are you doing?" Try again when the activity changes. If the child is ready, expand a single action word into a short phrase, turning "coloring" into "I'm coloring" or "playing" into "playing cars." Sentence expansion is optional and not required for success.
group_play_line: Take turns asking each child what they are doing. One child can also watch the other and say the action.
what_to_avoid: Do not interrupt deeply focused play just to ask the question, and do not ask repeatedly if the child does not answer.

title: Photo Actions
theme: Naming actions in photos of familiar people
materials: Two or three photos of familiar people doing clear everyday actions, such as eating, drinking, reading, sleeping, brushing teeth, coloring, or playing.
instructions: Choose photos your child is interested in, especially pictures of themselves, siblings, parents, grandparents, or other familiar people. Look at one photo together. Point to the person and ask, "What is Mama doing?" or "What are you doing here?" Pause for a few seconds. Accept any word or approximation connected to the action, then model the action clearly: "Eating!" Talk briefly about the picture, then move to another photo if your child is interested.
success_criteria: The child attempts to say the action shown in at least one photo.
make_easier: Start with only two very familiar photos showing obvious actions. Offer two choices if needed, such as "Is Papa eating or sleeping?" or "Are you coloring or drinking?" If the child chooses correctly without saying the action, acknowledge the understanding, model the action word, and give another opportunity to say it.
make_harder: Use a new photo that has not been practiced before, or a photo with fewer obvious visual clues. Ask the open action question without choices. If action labeling is already easy, briefly expand the conversation afterward, but keep action labeling as the primary target.
group_play_line: Let a sibling choose a family photo and ask what the person is doing, then switch roles.
what_to_avoid: Do not work through a large stack of photos like flash cards. Use a few meaningful pictures and keep the interaction natural.

title: Picture Book Actions
theme: Naming actions while looking at a favorite book
materials: A picture book with clear pictures of people or animals doing familiar actions.
instructions: Choose a book your child already enjoys. While reading together, stop naturally on a page where one character is clearly doing something. Point to the character and ask, "What is he doing?" or "What is she doing?" Pause for a few seconds. Accept any word or approximation connected to the action, then model the action clearly. Continue reading and try another action picture when it comes up naturally.
success_criteria: The child attempts to say the action shown in at least one picture.
make_easier: Choose a page with one clear character doing one obvious action. You may name the action first, then return to the same picture and ask again. You can also offer two choices, such as "Is she eating or sleeping?" If the child chooses nonverbally, that demonstrates understanding but does not count as expressive success. Model the action word and give another opportunity to say it.
make_harder: Use a new page your child has not practiced before, or a page with more than one thing happening. Ask the child to choose one person or animal and tell you what they are doing. If action labeling is easy, expand the word into a short sentence, turning "eating" into "The girl is eating." Sentence expansion remains optional.
group_play_line: Take turns choosing a character and asking what that person or animal is doing.
what_to_avoid: Do not stop on every page to ask questions or turn reading into a quiz. If the child does not know the action, model it and keep enjoying the story.

title: Pick One Action
theme: Finding and naming actions in a busy picture
materials: A picture book, magazine, or scene showing several people or animals doing different things.
instructions: Choose a picture with several things happening. Let your child pick one person or animal they are interested in. Point to that person and ask, "What are they doing?" Pause for a few seconds. Accept any word or approximation connected to the action, then model the action clearly. If your child is still interested, choose one more person in the same picture and ask again.
success_criteria: The child attempts to say the action for at least one person or animal in the picture.
make_easier: Start with a picture where one action is very obvious. Point directly to the person and offer two choices if needed, such as "Is she eating or sleeping?" If the child chooses correctly without saying the action, model the action word and give another opportunity to say it.
make_harder: Ask the child to name two different actions happening in the same picture, for example "The boy is eating. What is the girl doing?" If that becomes easy, let the child choose which people to talk about instead of you pointing first.
group_play_line: Take turns choosing someone in the picture. One child points and the other names the action.
what_to_avoid: Do not ask about many people at once or expect the child to describe the whole picture. Focus on one action first and add a second only when the first feels easy.

title: Action Charades
theme: Guessing and naming actions through pretend play
instructions: Tell your child you are going to play an action guessing game. Act out one familiar action without saying the action word, such as pretending to sleep, eat, drink, read, brush your teeth, wash your hands, clap, or wave. Ask, "What am I doing?" and pause. Accept any word or approximation connected to the action, then model the action clearly. Then switch roles. Let your child act something out while you guess. Continue taking turns while the game stays fun.
success_criteria: The child attempts to say at least one action word while guessing an action.
make_easier: Use a very familiar action and give two spoken choices if needed, such as "Am I sleeping or eating?" You can also demonstrate the action once while naming it, then act it again and give the child another opportunity to name it.
make_harder: Do not give choices. Let your child identify the action independently. You can also let your child choose and act out an action without telling you what it is first.
group_play_line: One child acts while the other guesses, then they switch roles.
what_to_avoid: Do not keep repeating the same action until the child produces the word. If they are unsure, model the action word and move to another turn.

title: Mini Action Story
theme: Naming actions while making a simple story
materials: Two or three family photos, book pictures, or simple pictures showing familiar actions.
instructions: Choose two or three pictures with clear familiar actions. Put the pictures in front of your child and make a tiny story together, for example "Papa is eating. The dog is sleeping. Maya is reading." Point to one picture and pause before saying the action: "Papa is...?" Give your child a chance to say the action word. Accept any word or approximation connected to the action, then model the action clearly and continue the little story. Let your child choose which picture comes next if they want.
success_criteria: The child attempts to say at least one action word while helping with the story.
make_easier: Start with only two very clear pictures. Name the person first and offer two spoken action choices, such as "Is Papa eating or sleeping?" If the child chooses without saying the word, model the action and give another opportunity to say it. Then you may repeat the complete sentence together: "Papa is eating."
make_harder: Use two pictures showing the same person doing two related actions, such as washing hands and then drying hands, getting dressed and then putting on shoes, eating and then drinking, or coloring and then putting the crayons away. Look at the first picture and ask, "What is she doing?" Then look at the second picture and ask, "What is she doing now?" After the child labels both actions, model the sequence: "First she is washing. Then she is drying." The main goal remains naming each action. Understanding the order, producing "first" and "then", or retelling the sequence is an optional extension and must not be required for success. Another harder variation may use three pictures with different familiar actions and let the child help choose the order for a silly mini story.
group_play_line: Take turns choosing a picture and adding one action to the story.
what_to_avoid: Do not require the child to remember a long sequence or tell an entire story independently. Keep the story short and playful, and support the action words as needed.
